newsitem.title: USA: Blacks left without voice on Miami city commission.
newsitem.headline: Blacks left without voice on Miami city commission.

text.p: A Cuban-American took office as a city commissioner Friday after defeating a black election opponent, and one black leader said the change was likely to feed frustration and resentment in this melting-pot city.
Humberto Hernandez, who was sworn in Friday, beat Richard Dunn 61 to 39 percent in Thursday's election, leaving Miami with no black commissioner for the first time in 30 years.
Hernandez acknowledged at his victory party in the Little Havana district Thursday night that blacks would feel they no longer had anyone to represent them.

"One of the first things I'm going to do is hold an emergency meeting with African American leaders and reassure them I will represent them so they don't feel left out," he told reporters. "I will fight for that community like I will for the rest of the community."

The seat on the five-person commission has unofficially but traditionally been a "black seat." It became vacant when Commissioner Miller Dawkins left in September in a corruption scandal. He has pleaded guilty to bribery charges and awaits sentencing.

Hernandez's victory marked another step in the ascendency of Miami's Hispanic community. Hispanics now are 49 percent of voters and blacks 27 percent. In October, Alex Penelas, also a Cuban American, was elected Miami's first executive mayor.

"There wasn't a great deal of surprise about the result because the numbers were there although there was a hope the Hispanic candidates would drop out," Lloyd Major, director of community relations at the Office of Black Affairs, said.

"The message to blacks is that on our own we won't ever have a successful vote. There is frustration this is just one more indication that we haven't reached that point yet. There's anger and anxiety in all this that has to do with economic conditions," Major told Reuters.

The history of Miami is scarred by racial tensions and periodic outbreaks of violence. Blacks have watched as Hispanics have prospered in business while new Latin immigrants have eagerly taken low-paying jobs.
Hernandez said he was in favour of dividing the city into electoral districts to ensure blacks had a better chance of electing a represenative. He pledged to make it a priority.
"That certainly is a step. There should be a voice for all the people," Major said. "The longer it waits the greater the chance of increased frustration."

Miami's run-off election was closely watched by city leaders after a race riot erupted Wednesday across the state in St. Petersburg when a grand jury refused to prosecute a white policeman for the fatal shooting of a black teenager.
